newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian economic reformers try to show who's boss.
newsitem.headline: Russian economic reformers try to show who's boss.

text.p: Russia's reformists, increasingly influential but worried economic changes are at a make-or-break stage, plan to show the opposition-led parliament who is boss by slashing spending this summer, economists said on Tuesday.

But parliament, even as deputies break for summer recess, could still throw a spanner into Moscow's austerity plans, as deputies head to constituencies in regions where impoverished voters are tired of tight purses and want wages and pensions.

"It's being said that if the Duma doesn't cut spending, the government will do so by decree," said Catherine MacDougall, a Russia analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London. "The point is that the government is not going to be stopped on this one."

The debate between reformers and parliament over the spending cuts, which could total nearly $20 trillion and affect everything from salaries to funding for industrial enterprises, have become a barometer of just how tough Russia's 100-day-old, fresh-faced cabinet is willing to get.

The State Duma lower chamber rejected on Monday a government proposal to cut 1997 spending by a whopping 108 trillion roubles ($19 billion), one fifth of the total, as well as an opposition bill for smaller cuts. It also threw out on Tuesday five government-sponsored draft laws aimed at cutting welfare benefits, approving a sixth after ministers made concessions.
No great defeat, emerging markets analysts said -- as long as the tight spending which ministers have vowed to enact, with or without parliament, helped to spur investment and growth.
"Politics aside, the operation of a budget on a real basis is a plus," said one Western economist, referring to the fact ministers were committed to spending less no matter what.
"But even though a lot of the fundamentals are in place, there's broad economic stagnation."

The face of the Russian economy has acquired a new glow in recent months with Russia's hugely successful, third, $2 billion Eurobond, an upbeat assessment at the Group of Seven richest industrialised nations summit and a booming stock market.
The yearly inflation rate, already down to a record low of 14.6 percent in May, is much healthier than the triple-digit levels of a little over a year ago.

The government is gunning for an annual rate of five percent in 1998 and will make the cost of borrowing even cheaper by pushing yields on government securities down to 12 percent from today's 20 percent.
But the economy also has a darker pallor from its struggle to emerge from seven years of severe contraction. The budget deficit is seen as the biggest threat yet to stabilisation.

Gross domestic product (GDP), the broadest measure of economic activity, slipped 0.2 percent in the first five months of this year compared to a year earlier and is forecast to fall two percent in 1997. Portfolio and direct investment are nudging up, but Russian savers still shift dollars out of the country.

First Deputy Prime Ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov -- the boy wonders of the new market-minded Russia and the drivers of its reforms -- have said spending cuts, along with reforming natural monopolies and cracking down on tax debtors, are the keys to real growth taking place in 1998.
"The government's going to go ahead with the cuts anyway -- Chubais has said if the money's not there, it can't be spent," said Eastern Europe analyst Charles Robertson.
"But there are still some dangers here -- at what point will the population get upset about wage arrears and lose faith in democracy?"
Chubais is a hate-figure for the opposition, which virulently opposes cuts in Soviet-style bottomless-pocket social subsidies.

He and Nemtsov, worried about the effect of perilously low tax revenues on economic and political stability, have moved Russia into new territory by threatening debtors with bankrupty, pushing a corporate-friendly tax code through parliament and persuading privatisation officials to speed up sell-offs.

"It's not a painless process and we're moving in the right direction and rather swiftly," MacDougall said. "But unless things are done swiftly, the economy is not going to grow, and then you can get back to a politically sensitive situation."
